extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners and patent practitioners (applicants, patent attorneys/agents)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for evaluating obviousness rejections (35 U.S.C. 103) including overlapping ranges, optimization, genus/species issues, and rebuttal evidence. Instructs examiners on articulated rationale, Graham factors, and how applicants may rebut prima facie obviousness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Overlapping, approaching, and similar ranges, amounts, and proportions
rubrics_metrics.description: In the case where the claimed ranges “overlap or lie inside ranges disclosed by the prior art” a prima facie case of obviousness exists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case law examples: In re Wertheim; In re Woodruff (prior art "about 1-5%" allowed concentrations slightly above 5%); In re Geisler (thickness ranges). If ranges overlap, prima facie obviousness is established. But consider if the prior art range is so broad as to encompass many distinct compositions (analogous to genus issues). See MPEP § 2131.03 and § 2144.08.

rubrics_metrics.name: Close but non-overlapping ranges may be prima facie obvious
rubrics_metrics.description: A prima facie case of obviousness exists where the claimed ranges or amounts do not overlap with the prior art but are merely close.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Titanium Metals Corp. v. Banner — proportions so close that one skilled in the art would have expected the same properties. Courts have found close numeric proximity sufficient absent evidence of unexpected results or criticality (In re Brandt).

rubrics_metrics.name: Broad prior-art ranges may be analogous to a genus and alter obviousness analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: If the reference’s disclosed range is so broad as to encompass a very large number of possible distinct compositions, this might present a situation analogous to the obviousness of a species when the prior art broadly discloses a genus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See In re Baird, In re Jones, and MPEP § 2144.08. When a prior-art range is extremely broad, additional analysis is needed because a genus disclosure does not automatically render every species obvious.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ranges disclosed across multiple prior-art references can establish a prior-art 'range'
rubrics_metrics.description: A range can be disclosed in multiple prior art references instead of in a single prior art reference depending on the specific facts of the case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Iron Grip Barbell Co. v. USA Sports — multiple prior patents disclosing 1, 2 or 4 openings led to presumption that 3 openings fell within the prior-art range. The 'range' disclosed in multiple references is functionally equivalent to a single-reference disclosure for range analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Routine optimization does not support patentability absent criticality
rubrics_metrics.description: Generally, differences in concentration or temperature will not support the patentability of subject matter encompassed by the prior art unless there is evidence indicating such concentration or temperature is critical.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discovering optimum or workable ranges by routine experimentation is not inventive (In re Aller, Peterson, In re Hoeschele). See KSR v. Teleflex for caution about granting patents based on combinations found in prior art. If claimed ranges fall within broad prior art scope, examiner should look for evidence of criticality or unexpected results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examiner must articulate a rationale supporting a routine-optimization rejection
rubrics_metrics.description: In order to properly support a rejection on the basis that an invention is the result of 'routine optimization', the examiner must make findings of relevant facts and present the underpinning reasoning in sufficient detail.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The articulated rationale must explain why it would have been routine optimization to arrive at the claimed invention and why a person of ordinary skill would have had a reasonable expectation of success to formulate the claimed range. See In re Stepan; Arendi v. Apple; In re Van Os. Mere statements of 'common sense' without reasoned analysis are insufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: "Obvious to try" can be a valid rationale in appropriate circumstances
rubrics_metrics.description: "Obvious to try" reasoning may properly support an obviousness rejection when there is a design need or market demand and a finite number of identified, predictable solutions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: KSR v. Teleflex held that when there is a design need and a finite set of predictable solutions, 'obvious to try' can show obviousness. Contrast with pre-KSR Antonie which required recognition of a result-effective variable; after KSR the presence of a known result-effective variable is one but not the only motivation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rebuttal by showing the range is critical (unexpected results)
rubrics_metrics.description: Applicants can rebut a prima facie case of obviousness by showing the criticality of the range, generally by showing that the claimed range achieves unexpected results relative to the prior art range.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite In re Woodruff, Minerals Separation v. Hyde, In re Scherl, etc. The applicant bears the burden to establish criticality by proper factual showing. See MPEP § 716.02 - § 716.02(g) for further discussion on criticality and unexpected results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rebuttal by showing that the prior art teaches away
rubrics_metrics.description: A prima facie case of obviousness may be rebutted by showing that the art, in any material respect, teaches away from the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authorities: U.S. v. Adams; Depuy Spine v. Medtronic; Allergan v. Sandoz. Example In re Geisler: court found that a reference did not teach away despite expressing preference for thicker coatings because it provided motivation to explore thinner layers. See MPEP § 2145 subsection X.D. for 'teaching away' discussion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rebuttal by showing the claimed parameter was not recognized as 'result-effective'
rubrics_metrics.description: Applicants may rebut a prima facie case by showing that the claimed variable was not recognized in the prior art to be a result-effective variable (i.e., the prior art did not indicate that changing that variable affects the result).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Antonie described the 'result-effective variable' exception; it's narrow. E.I. DuPont de Nemours v. Synvina and Applied Materials discuss that lack of any prior-art disclosure of a relationship between the variable and result supports this rebuttal. Applicants must articulate why the variable would not have been recognized as result-effective in the prior art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combining equivalents known for the same purpose is prima facie obvious
rubrics_metrics.description: It is prima facie obvious to combine two compositions each of which is taught by the prior art to be useful for the same purpose in order to form a third composition to be used for the same purpose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In re Kerkhoven; In re Crockett; Ex parte Quadranti — combining known items taught for the same purpose 'flows logically' from their individual teachings. Use these precedents when combination merely mixes known materials with known utility for the same end.

rubrics_metrics.name: Substituting equivalents known for the same purpose requires art-recognized equivalency
rubrics_metrics.description: To rely on equivalence as a rationale supporting an obviousness rejection, the equivalency must be recognized in the prior art and cannot be based solely on applicant’s disclosure or mere functional equivalence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In re Ruff and Smith v. Hayashi: mere membership in a Markush group or functional equivalence is insufficient; evidence that elements were known photoconductors (for example) can support substituting one for another. An express suggestion to substitute is not always necessary (In re Fout).

rubrics_metrics.name: Very broad prior-art ranges may weaken ordinary motivation to optimize
rubrics_metrics.description: One factor weighing against an obviousness rejection based on optimization is where the prior art disclosure of the variable is within a range so broad, in light of dissimilar characteristics of members, that it would not invite optimization by one of skill in the art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Genetics Inst. v. Novartis — disclosure of 68,000 protein variants made ordinary motivation to optimize inapplicable. See MPEP §§ 2131.02, 2131.03, and 2144.08 for additional discussion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not apply per se rules when genus disclosed and claimed species differ
rubrics_metrics.description: The fact that a claimed species or subgenus is encompassed by a prior-art genus is not sufficient by itself to establish a prima facie case of obviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow In re Baird, In re Jones, and related precedent: analyze patentability under 35 U.S.C. 103 on the facts of the particular case; do not apply per se rules that a genus disclosure automatically renders species obvious.

rubrics_metrics.name: When a single prior-art reference discloses a genus, seek additional prior art and analyze specific factors
rubrics_metrics.description: When a single prior art reference discloses a genus encompassing the claimed species/subgenus but does not expressly disclose the claimed species, Office personnel should attempt to find additional prior art; absent additional art, consider specific factors to determine if a single-reference 103 rejection is appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If no additional art is found, evaluate the structure of the genus and species, physical/chemical properties and utilities, predictability of the technology, and the number of species encompassed by the genus (MPEP § 2144.08 II).

rubrics_metrics.name: Determine the scope and content of the prior art (Graham factor A)
rubrics_metrics.description: Office personnel should determine the scope and content of the relevant prior art. Each reference must qualify as prior art under 35 U.S.C. 102 and must be analogous art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See Panduit Corp. v. Dennison for requirement that references be prior art under §102. Use MPEP § 2141.01(a) for analogous art guidance. For a genus disclosure, make findings on (A)-(D) described in §2144.08.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ascertain the differences between the prior art and the claims (Graham factor B)
rubrics_metrics.description: Compare the claimed species/subgenus to the closest disclosed prior-art species/subgenus to determine similarities and differences in structure, properties, and utilities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify the closest disclosed species and make explicit findings on similarities/differences. The issue under §103 is whether the claimed invention as a whole would have been obvious (Stratoflex).

rubrics_metrics.name: Determine the level of ordinary skill in the pertinent art (Graham factor C)
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate the relevant prior art from the standpoint of a hypothetical person having ordinary skill in the art at the time the claimed invention was made.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the prior art to infer level of skill; consider any applicant-submitted evidence. Authorities: Ryko Mfg. Co. v. Nu-Star; Uniroyal v. Rudkin-Wiley. See MPEP §§ 2141 and 2141.03 for guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate evidence of secondary considerations (Graham factor D)
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate any evidence of secondary considerations (objective indicia) such as commercial success, long-felt need, copying, etc., when determining obviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a prima facie case is established, the burden shifts to applicant to rebut with evidence/argument. Secondary considerations must be considered in the totality of circumstances (Graham, In re Bell, Rijckaert, Oetiker). Example: Iron Grip Barbell — applicant failed to show nexus for licensing, copying, or long-felt need.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determine whether one of ordinary skill would have been motivated to select the claimed species
rubrics_metrics.description: After analyzing Graham factors, determine if it would have been obvious for a person of ordinary skill to select the claimed species/subgenus from the prior-art genus, considering all relevant prior-art teachings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus on the size of the genus (but do not apply per se rules), predictability, prior-art teachings, and totality of circumstances. A very small genus may render members envisagable (Petering). Make explicit findings about motivation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make explicit factual findings when relying on a genus-to-species obviousness rationale
rubrics_metrics.description: Office personnel should make findings as to (A) structure of prior-art genus and species, (B) physical/chemical properties and utilities disclosed for the genus, (C) predictability of the technology, and (D) number of species encompassed by the genus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These findings inform whether the selection of the claimed species from a genus would have been obvious. Use these findings before concluding a prima facie genus-to-species obviousness rejection.
